result.summary: This section gathers fragments of Hesiod's Catalogue of Women. It opens with a winter-storm passage about a hibernating serpent, then offers quoted lines and testimonies on the houses of Atreus, Minos, Theseus, Eurytus, Locrus and others.

scenes.title: Storm and the hibernating serpent
scenes.summary: A fierce wind sent by Zeus blasts the trees and crops. A serpent, the Hairless One, lives in the mountains in spring and in a cave in winter, and is struck down by the arrows of Zeus.
scenes.stakes: Mankind's crops and strength fail in the storm; the serpent is laid low by Zeus.

scenes.title: Atreus' line, Iphigeneia, Butes, Sicyon
scenes.summary: Scholars cite Hesiod on the descent of Agamemnon and Menelaus, Helen's children, Iphigeneia becoming Hecate, Butes as son of Poseidon, and Sicyon as son of Erechtheus.

scenes.title: Minos, Eurygyes, Theseus, Cychreus
scenes.summary: Fragments describe Minos as most kingly, the honouring of Eurygyes at Athens, Theseus' desertion of Ariadne for Aegle, and the snake of Cychreus received by Demeter at Eleusis.

scenes.title: Heracles' circle, Locrus, Ileus
scenes.summary: Fragments mention Iolaus as Heracles' charioteer, the family of Eurytus, Autolycus, Aepytus' sons, the making of people from stones for Deucalion, and Apollo's love for Ileus.

alias_notes.explanation: Androgeos son of Minos was also called Eurygyes.
A footnoted epithet for the hibernating serpent.

notable_quotes.reason: Records the variant tradition that Iphigeneia was not sacrificed but became Hecate.
Gives a pun-based origin of people (laoi) from stones (laas).

analysis.text: The fragments show the Catalogue's genealogical method, tying heroes and cities to divine and heroic ancestors.
These survive only as quotations by later scholars, and sources note ancient claims of interpolation, such as Peisistratus supposedly removing a verse.

legacy.text: The variant of Iphigeneia's rescue and transformation influenced later versions, such as Euripides' Iphigeneia among the Taurians, where she is saved by Artemis.

fun_facts.text: Fragment 82 plays on Greek laoi, 'people', and laas, 'stone', in Deucalion's tale.

language_notes.text: Boreas is the North Wind, personified as a god in Greek tradition.
"The Hairless One" is a riddling name for the serpent, likely a kenning-like periphrasis; the footnote marks it as obscure.
"Soul" here is the shade or ghost left after death, which flits and gibbers like the dead in Homer.
A lacuna is a gap where the manuscript or papyrus text is lost.
Hesiod and Aeschylus make Agamemnon and Menelaus sons of Pleisthenes, not directly of Atreus as in Homer.
Alludes to the usual myth of Iphigeneia's sacrifice at Aulis; Hesiod's variant has Artemis save her and make her Hecate.
Plato's dialogue Minos quotes this line from Hesiod to show Minos' reputation as a ruler; the page number is a reference to the standard edition.
"Sceptre of Zeus" means kingly authority believed to be granted by Zeus; the translator uses the spelling Zeus here.
Peisistratus, tyrant of Athens, was accused of removing lines unflattering to Theseus, an Athenian hero; Hereas of Megara, a hostile neighbour, made the charge.
The island is Salamis, which Cychreus ruled; the snake was said to have infested it before Demeter took it to Eleusis.
Lelegian: the Leleges were an ancient people of Greece and Asia Minor, here led by Locrus.
The wordplay depends on Greek: laos (people) resembles laas (stone), so people are "made from stones" after Deucalion's flood.
Complaisant means willing and agreeable; here the nymph consents to love.

context_notes.text: Tzetzes was a twelfth-century Byzantine scholar whose commentaries preserve many fragments of lost early Greek poetry.
Pausanias was a second-century AD Greek travel writer who often cites Hesiod's lost Catalogue.
Eustathius was a twelfth-century archbishop of Thessalonica who wrote huge commentaries on Homer.
Androgeos, son of Minos, was killed in Attica, which led Minos to demand tribute from Athens; funeral games honoured him.
Ariadne helped Theseus escape the Minotaur's labyrinth and was afterwards left by him.
Iolaus was Heracles' nephew and charioteer; the argument uses this detail to attribute the Shield to Hesiod.
Iphitus is called a scion of Ares, meaning a descendant of the war god, a mark of warlike lineage.
Autolycus was a legendary master thief, son of Hermes in later tradition, famed for making stolen goods unrecognizable.

literary_notes.text: The deep "seethed" and all things "trembled", giving the storm a living, menacing force driven by Zeus's will.
Piled leaves and a spotted back make the serpent's winter hiding place vivid and sinister.
Zeus's arrows, a thunderbolt image, show divine power punishing excess.
"Most kingly of mortal kings" is a superlative formula that fixes Minos' reputation as an ideal ruler.
Love is described as a force that "overpowered" Theseus, presenting desire as an active conqueror of the hero.
"God-like Toxeus" uses a stock Homeric-style adjective to elevate the heroic sons.
Making everything he touched vanish exaggerates Autolycus' thieving skill into something almost magical.
